questions.question: The first Christmas card sold in Britain, in 1843, caused a small scandal. Why?
options: It poked fun at Queen Victoria
It was printed entirely in German
It showed a family, child included, raising glasses of wine
questions.explanation: The civil servant Henry Cole was too busy to write his usual Christmas letters, so he asked the artist John Callcott Horsley to design a card. About a thousand were printed and sold at a shilling each. The centre panel showed a merry family toasting the season, a small child included, and the temperance movement was not amused. Cole later became the founding director of what is now the V&A.

questions.question: In 1897 eight-year-old Virginia O’Hanlon wrote to a New York newspaper with a question. The famous reply began “Yes, Virginia, there is a…”
questions.explanation: Her friends had told her Santa wasn’t real, and her father said, “If you see it in The Sun, it’s so.” The New York Sun answered her in an unsigned editorial on 21 September 1897, so not at Christmas at all. The writer, Francis Pharcellus Church, was named only after his death. It became the most reprinted editorial in the history of English-language newspapers.

questions.question: In 1848 a magazine picture of a royal family gathered round a decorated tree made the Christmas tree a must-have in Britain. Which royal couple was it?
options: King George III and Queen Charlotte
King Edward VII and Queen Alexandra
King William IV and Queen Adelaide
questions.explanation: The Illustrated London News showed Victoria, Albert and their children around a tabletop tree at Windsor, and soon every fashionable household wanted one. Albert usually gets the credit for bringing the custom from Germany, but George III’s German-born wife, Queen Charlotte, had set one up at Windsor as early as 1800. When an American magazine reprinted the picture in 1850, it quietly removed the Queen’s tiara and Albert’s moustache so the family would pass for Americans.

questions.question: The Christmas cracker was invented in the 1840s by a London sweet-maker. What was wrapped inside the very first ones?
questions.explanation: Tom Smith sold sugared almonds wrapped in a twist of paper with a love motto tucked inside, an idea he picked up from French bon-bons. The bang came later, reputedly inspired by the crackle of a log fire. Eventually the sweet was dropped altogether in favour of paper hats, small trinkets and, yes, the terrible jokes.

questions.question: In 1647 England’s Puritan-led Parliament did something drastic to Christmas. What?
questions.explanation: Parliament abolished Christmas, Easter and Whitsun as feast days, and that December there were pro-Christmas riots in Canterbury and elsewhere. Oliver Cromwell usually takes the blame, though he did not become Lord Protector until 1653. Christmas came back legally with the return of the monarchy in 1660.

questions.question: “Silent Night” was first sung on Christmas Eve 1818. In which country?
questions.explanation: It was first sung as “Stille Nacht” in the village church of Oberndorf, near Salzburg. The young priest Joseph Mohr wrote the words, and the schoolteacher Franz Xaver Gruber wrote the tune. The two performed it with a guitar. The popular story that mice had chewed through the organ is a later embellishment.

questions.question: In the first printing of “’Twas the Night Before Christmas”, in 1823, two of the reindeer were called Dunder and Blixem. What do those old Dutch-style names mean?
questions.explanation: The poem, properly titled “A Visit from St. Nicholas”, appeared anonymously in a New York newspaper on 23 December 1823. The names were later changed to Donder and Blitzen, and eventually Donner, which are the German words for thunder and lightning. Clement Clarke Moore claimed the poem years later, though some historians believe Henry Livingston Jr. wrote it.

questions.question: In the 1860s the cartoonist Thomas Nast drew Santa for Harper’s Weekly and gave him a permanent home. Where?
questions.explanation: Before Nast, nobody was quite sure where Santa lived. Nast also gave us Santa’s workshop and his book of good and naughty children. His very first Santa, in January 1863, showed him in a stars-and-stripes jacket handing out presents to Union soldiers in the Civil War.

questions.question: In “The Twelve Days of Christmas”, what does my true love send on the fifth day?
questions.explanation: Singers traditionally stretch out “five go-old rings” for a reason: it is the turning point of the song. If you add up every gift across all twelve days, counting the repeats, the total is 364, one for every day of the year bar one.

questions.question: In A Christmas Carol, what bird do the Cratchits have for Christmas dinner?
questions.explanation: Mrs Cratchit’s goose is a modest bird stretched across a large family, with apple sauce and mashed potatoes. Once Scrooge has changed his ways, he sends them the prize turkey from the poulterer’s, “twice the size of Tiny Tim”. In Victorian times goose was the usual celebration bird; turkey only became the standard English Christmas dinner in the twentieth century.

questions.question: Tinsel was first made in Germany in the early 1600s. What was it made from?
questions.explanation: Silver was hammered thin and cut into strips. It looked splendid by candlelight, but it soon tarnished. Cheaper metals followed, then aluminium, and finally the plastic tinsel we know today. The word comes from an Old French word meaning “spark”.

questions.question: The poinsettia, the red-leaved Christmas plant, originally comes from which country?
questions.explanation: The Aztecs called it cuetlaxochitl and used it to make red dye. Its English name honours Joel Roberts Poinsett, the first American ambassador to Mexico, who sent cuttings home to South Carolina in the 1820s. In the United States, 12 December is National Poinsettia Day, marking the date of his death.

questions.question: The first electric Christmas tree lights were strung up in 1882 by a business partner of which famous inventor?
questions.explanation: Edward H. Johnson, Edison’s partner, hand-wired 80 red, white and blue bulbs onto a slowly revolving tree in his New York parlour. For years electric lights were a rich family’s novelty, and most people kept using real candles on their trees, fire buckets at the ready.

questions.question: In December 1965 two astronauts surprised Mission Control by playing “Jingle Bells” on a smuggled harmonica and bells. Where were they?
options: On the ship that picked them up
questions.explanation: Wally Schirra and Tom Stafford first reported sighting a mysterious “satellite” piloted by a man in a red suit, then broke into “Jingle Bells”, making it the first song played in space. The song itself dates from 1857, when it was published as “The One Horse Open Sleigh”. It never actually mentions Christmas.

questions.question: “Good King Wenceslas looked out, on the Feast of Stephen.” What is that day better known as in Britain?
questions.explanation: The Feast of St Stephen falls on 26 December. In the carol the king spots a poor man gathering firewood and sets out through the snow to bring him food and drink, which suits a day long associated with giving to those in need. The real Wenceslas was a tenth-century Duke of Bohemia; the title of king came only after his death. The words were written by John Mason Neale in 1853.

questions.question: When Victorians went “wassailing”, what were they doing?
options: Going door to door singing and drinking toasts
questions.explanation: “Wassail” comes from the Old English for “be in good health”. Wassailers carried a bowl of hot spiced ale or cider from house to house, sang, and expected a drink or a coin in return, as in “Here we come a-wassailing”. In cider country people also wassailed the apple trees, toasting them for a good harvest.

questions.question: Saturnalia, a December festival of feasting, parties and gift-giving, began on 17 December. Who celebrated it?
questions.explanation: Saturnalia began on this very day and eventually stretched to a week. Togas were swapped for party clothes, gambling was allowed in public, masters sometimes waited on their servants, and friends gave each other small gifts such as candles and little clay figures. The poet Catullus called it “the best of days”.

questions.question: The Nutcracker ballet premiered in St Petersburg on 18 December 1892. Who composed the music?
questions.explanation: Tchaikovsky’s ballet got a lukewarm reception at first. For the Dance of the Sugar Plum Fairy he used the celesta, a tinkling keyboard instrument he had found in Paris, and asked his publisher to keep it secret so that no rival composer would use it first. The ballet became a Christmas tradition mostly in America after the Second World War.

questions.question: A Christmas Carol was published on this day in 1843. What is Scrooge’s first name?
questions.explanation: Jacob is Marley, Bob is Cratchit and Fred is Scrooge’s cheerful nephew. Dickens paid to have the book printed with gilt edges and hand-coloured illustrations. All 6,000 copies of the first edition sold out by Christmas Eve, but the costs were so high that he made only about £230.

questions.question: How many ghosts visit Scrooge in A Christmas Carol, counting Jacob Marley?
questions.explanation: Marley comes first, in chains, to warn Scrooge that three spirits will follow: the Ghosts of Christmas Past, Present and Yet to Come. In keeping with the idea of a carol, Dickens called the book’s five chapters “staves”, an old word for the verses of a song.

questions.question: Victorian etiquette had a rule for kissing under the mistletoe. What was it?
options: Pick one berry for each kiss, and stop when the berries run out
The kiss must be on the hand
The gentleman must first bow three times
questions.explanation: Once the berries were gone, the mistletoe lost its power. The plant’s Christmas reputation is ancient: in Norse myth the god Baldr was killed by a dart of mistletoe, the one thing his mother had forgotten to make promise never to harm him.

questions.question: True or false: Coca-Cola advertisements from 1931 gave Santa his red suit.
options: False. Red-suited Santas had been around for decades.
questions.explanation: Santa wears red on magazine covers from the early 1900s and on a great many Victorian and Edwardian Christmas cards. Some older cards show him in green, brown or blue, which is how the myth took hold. What the Coca-Cola artist Haddon Sundblom did fix was the warm, chubby, grandfatherly face we picture today.

questions.question: Every year since 1947 Norway has given London the Christmas tree in Trafalgar Square. Why?
options: As thanks for Britain’s help in the Second World War
questions.explanation: During the war Norway’s king and government carried on the fight from exile in London. The tree, a Norway spruce from the forests around Oslo, is decorated in the Norwegian style, with simple strings of white lights running straight down.

questions.question: On Christmas Eve 1906 the inventor Reginald Fessenden is said to have broadcast one of the first radio programmes of music, to ships at sea. Which carol did he play on the violin?
questions.explanation: Radio operators who had only ever heard Morse code suddenly heard a violin. By Fessenden’s own later account he played “O Holy Night”, sang the last verse, and read “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will toward men.” Historians aren’t certain it happened just as he told it, but it makes a fine end to the calendar. Rudolph arrived in 1939 and White Christmas in 1942. A merry Christmas to you.
